overview.summary: Nuclear fission is among the lowest-carbon and lowest-death electricity sources, yet Western projects run chronically over budget and behind schedule, leaving open whether it should be central to decarbonization or a costly detour.
overview.scope_covered: Commercial fission electricity: the existing reactor fleet, plant restarts and license extensions, new large reactors (e.g. AP1000/Vogtle), and advanced/small modular reactors — assessed on cost, build speed, safety, waste, and their role versus renewables in a decarbonizing grid facing AI-driven demand growth.
overview.scope_excluded: Nuclear fusion; nuclear weapons and proliferation policy as a standalone subject; naval/military reactors; medical isotopes and non-power applications; detailed reactor engineering and fuel chemistry; exhaustive country-by-country policy accounts.
overview.why_now: An aging Western fleet meets surging electricity demand from AI data centers and electrification — tech firms have signed 10+ GW of nuclear deals (Microsoft's Three Mile Island restart, Amazon, Google, Meta's SMR RFPs) and climate targets need firm clean power — even as Vogtle's ~$36.8B final cost and NuScale's cancelled SMR sharpen the affordability question.

basics.intro: Seven facts almost every side of the nuclear debate accepts: measured against its record, nuclear is among the safest and lowest-carbon ways to make electricity and runs the existing fleet near flat-out — yet new Western builds arrive years late at multiples of budget, cost far more per MWh than wind or solar today, and leave high-level waste with no permanent home.

stats.label: Lifecycle carbon intensity of nuclear
stats.note: The IPCC AR5 median for nuclear is on par with wind and below solar, and roughly 70× lower than coal's ~820 gCO₂/kWh — making it a low-carbon source by any accounting.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data (IPCC AR5 lifecycle emissions)

stats.label: Death rate from nuclear electricity
stats.note: Including Chernobyl and Fukushima, nuclear sits in the same low band as wind (0.04) and solar (0.02) and roughly 800× below coal (24.6/TWh); the exact figure ranges ~0.03–0.07 with Fukushima death assumptions.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data — safest sources of energy

stats.label: Nuclear share of global electricity
stats.note: Nuclear supplied about 9% of global electricity in 2024 — its lowest share in over four decades even as absolute output rose ~4% — versus roughly 18–19% in the US and ~23% in the EU.

stats.label: US nuclear fleet capacity factor
stats.note: US reactors have run above a 90% capacity factor for two decades — the highest and most reliable of any generating source — meaning the existing fleet delivers firm power nearly around the clock.

stats.label: Vogtle 3 & 4 final cost vs. estimate
stats.note: America's only new reactors this century reached commercial operation (Unit 4, April 2024) at roughly $35 billion to the owners and about $36.8 billion all-in including financing — against an original ~$14 billion (2008) estimate and about seven years late, the emblematic case for chronic Western cost and schedule overruns.

stats.label: Levelized cost: new nuclear vs. renewables
stats.note: Lazard's 2024 unsubsidized LCOE puts new nuclear at roughly 3× utility solar ($29–92) and onshore wind ($27–73) per MWh — the core of the argument that dollars buy more decarbonization elsewhere today.

stats.label: US spent fuel with no permanent repository
stats.note: Over 90,000 tonnes of commercial spent fuel sits in pools and dry casks at reactor sites because the US has built no permanent geologic repository since the 2010 Yucca Mountain impasse — disposal solved in principle, unsolved in practice.

questions.text: Are runaway Western nuclear construction costs a fixable problem of lost expertise, one-off designs and regulation, or a structural feature of the technology?
questions.why: South Korea has built reactors for roughly $2,000-4,000/kW while recent Western projects ran years late and billions over — Vogtle ~$10,000/kW, Hinkley Point C now ~£48bn. The contest is causal: if the overruns trace to lost supply chains, first-of-a-kind one-off designs, stop-start programs and a regulatory ratchet, then reform and serial building could restore low costs; if they encode irreducible complexity or genuine democratic safety preferences, no process fix removes them. Empirical at root — a factual question about what actually drives the costs — though it shades into values about acceptable caution.

questions.text: Given finite dollars and time to cut emissions, should decarbonization prioritize nuclear or lean on renewables plus storage that are cheaper per MWh today?
questions.why: Utility-scale wind and solar undercut new-build nuclear on levelized cost per MWh today, yet nuclear delivers firm, weather-independent power. System models in the Jenkins/MIT vein find that adding firm low-carbon sources, including nuclear, lowers the total cost and risk of reaching zero emissions, while Jacobson-style analyses argue 100% wind-water-solar with storage and transmission is feasible — with Clack and others disputing those assumptions. The cost and system figures are empirical, but 'should prioritize' embeds a choice of objective — least cost per MWh now, firmness, land use, speed, or option value — and a portfolio strategy, so it resolves to a value judgment no single number settles.

questions.text: Can new nuclear — large reactors or SMRs — actually deploy at enough scale and speed to matter for 2050 climate targets and near-term AI demand?
questions.why: Solar added ~550-600 GW per year in 2024-2025 while nuclear added single-digit GW net, with new reactor construction not accelerating until the 2030s and most SMR designs still first-of-a-kind or unbuilt — an ~80-100x gap in current deployment pace. Advocates argue firm clean power will be needed regardless, that historical French and Korean programs prove fast ramps are possible, and that AI-driven demand and private capital can pull build rates up; skeptics argue the timelines and historical build records make a material mid-century contribution implausible. Achievable build rates and supply-chain capacity are measurable in principle; the disagreement is over forecasts, not values.

questions.text: Is high-level waste solved in principle by deep geological disposal but unsolved in practice, and how much should the practical gap weigh against nuclear?
questions.why: Deep geological disposal is widely regarded as technically sound, and Finland's Onkalo is moving into operation as the first repository for civilian spent fuel — yet decades in, most countries still have no sited repository, and the only long-operating deep store (WIPP) takes military transuranic waste, not spent fuel. Skeptics such as Ramana further argue repositories carry real long-timescale failure risk from canister corrosion and shifting geology. The dispute is partly factual but turns on a normative judgment — how much an unsolved-in-practice siting-and-trust problem, plus irreducible deep-time uncertainty, should count as the problem being genuinely unsolved.

questions.text: Do nuclear's tail risks — accidents, long-lived waste, proliferation — justify constraining it, given its very low measured death rate per TWh?
questions.why: By lifecycle deaths per unit of energy nuclear is among the safest sources, on par with wind and solar and far below fossil fuels, yet its harms are concentrated, dreaded, and span generations — rare meltdowns, proliferation pathways, and waste that outlasts the institutions meant to guard it. Some skeptics also contest the death statistics themselves, holding the Chernobyl and Fukushima tolls are undercounted. Even where the figures are agreed, people differ on whether low-probability, high-consequence, long-tail risks deserve a special precautionary standard or should be weighed on the same expected-value terms as any other hazard — a normative choice no dataset resolves.

positions.name: Climate Pragmatist
positions.steelman: The reactors we already have are our biggest source of clean, around-the-clock power — keeping them running and restarting the good ones is the cheapest, fastest carbon we can buy.
positions.description: The existing fleet already delivers roughly a fifth of U.S. electricity and more than half of its carbon-free generation, and every plant we retire early gets replaced mostly by gas or coal — Germany's shutdown pushed its lignite share up while France's nuclear grid stayed among Europe's cleanest. Extending a paid-off reactor's license to 60 or 80 years is, by the IEA's accounting, the single lowest-cost source of low-carbon electricity available, cheaper per MWh than building almost anything new. We don't have to win the reactor-cost argument to act: uprating, relicensing (Diablo Canyon), and restarting shuttered-but-sound plants (Palisades, Three Mile Island) deliver firm clean power now, with the lowest measured death rate per TWh of any major source. This isn't nuclear-versus-renewables — least-cost decarbonization models consistently include clean firm power alongside wind and solar, because batteries don't cover the long, windless, sunless stretches. Losing this fleet to premature closure is a self-inflicted climate wound we can't afford with demand rising.
positions.proponents: International Energy Agency (Fatih Birol), Jesse Jenkins (Princeton ZERO Lab), U.S. Department of Energy Loan Programs Office, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Constellation Energy (Joe Dominguez), American Nuclear Society, IAEA (Rafael Grossi)
positions.representative_name: IEA, "Nuclear Power and Secure Energy Transitions" (2022)
positions.representative_note: The IEA's flagship nuclear report frames lifetime extensions of the existing fleet as "an indispensable part of a cost-effective path to net zero" and the lowest-cost low-carbon option, positioning nuclear as a complement to renewables rather than a rival — the core of the pragmatist case.

positions.name: Cost Skeptic
positions.steelman: Nuclear works — but with finite dollars and years to cut carbon, every one spent on a reactor buys far more emissions cuts in wind, solar and storage, sooner.
positions.description: We're not against nuclear on principle; we're against wasting scarce decarbonization budgets on it. The physics works, but the economics don't: unsubsidized new nuclear runs roughly $140/MWh in Lazard's analysis while utility-scale solar and onshore wind land near $30–60, and a reactor takes 10–15 years from planning to power versus 1–3 for a wind or solar farm. Because you can't spend the same dollar twice, buying a costly, slow nuclear kilowatt-hour displaces several cheap, fast renewable ones — so nuclear saves less carbon, later, per dollar and per year. Firming intermittency with storage, transmission and demand response is now cheaper than closing the gap with new reactors, and those costs keep falling while nuclear's keep rising. In a race against the clock, the climate-optimal move is to deploy the cheapest, fastest tons of abatement first — and that isn't new nuclear.
positions.proponents: Amory Lovins (RMI), Mark Z. Jacobson (Stanford), Mycle Schneider (World Nuclear Industry Status Report), Lazard LCOE analysis, Michael Liebreich (BloombergNEF founder)
positions.representative_note: Lovins's "climate opportunity cost" argument: a nuclear kWh costs several times a renewable kWh and arrives a decade later, so the same money spent on renewables and efficiency displaces far more carbon, far sooner — laid out in his RMI work and 2019 Forbes essay "Does Nuclear Power Slow or Speed Climate Change?"

positions.name: New-Nuclear Advocate
positions.steelman: Stop building nuclear like cathedrals and start building it like airplanes — standardized, factory-made reactors ride a learning curve down, and AI-hungry hyperscalers plus private capital are finally paying to start the line.
positions.description: The reason Western reactors cost so much isn't physics — it's that we build each one as a bespoke megaproject, first-of-a-kind every time, with no serial production to learn from. Advanced and small modular reactors flip that: standardized, factory-fabricated designs built many times over unlock the same learning curve that made solar, batteries, and aircraft cheap, while smaller unit sizes cut construction time and the interest costs that bury large builds. For the first time we have the demand and the money to prime that pump — AI data centers are signing multi-gigawatt deals (Meta with TerraPower and Oklo, Amazon with X-energy, Google with Kairos), and private capital, not just utilities, is funding the first units. First-of-a-kind plants will be expensive, as they always are; the whole point is that the tenth and hundredth won't be. Bet big now to get down the curve, because firm, carbon-free, land-light power that a hyperscaler will buy on a 20-year contract is exactly what a decarbonizing, electrifying grid needs.
positions.proponents: Bill Gates and TerraPower (Natrium); Sam Altman and Jacob DeWitte, Oklo (Aurora); X-energy (Xe-100, backed by Amazon); Kairos Power (KP-FHR, backed by Google); NuScale Power; Rolls-Royce SMR; the Breakthrough Institute; the IEA's "The Path to a New Era for Nuclear Energy"
positions.representative_name: TerraPower (Natrium reactor), founded by Bill Gates
positions.representative_note: Building its first 345 MW sodium-cooled Natrium plant in Kemmerer, Wyoming, with a decoupled molten-salt storage design; cleared a final NRC safety evaluation in late 2025 and won Meta funding for two units by 2032 plus up to six more (~2.1 GW) by 2035 — a concrete test of the "standardize a design, then repeat it" thesis backed by private and hyperscaler capital.

positions.name: Risk-First Skeptic
positions.steelman: A technology whose worst day poisons land for centuries, breeds bomb material, and burdens ten thousand generations with our waste is not one whose average death rate you get to average away.
positions.description: Averaging deaths per terawatt-hour is exactly the wrong lens for a technology defined by its tails: Chernobyl and Fukushima each rendered whole regions uninhabitable and cost hundreds of billions, and no actuarial mean captures that. Those were operating-plant accidents, which is why this camp works to close the reactors we already run, not just to halt new ones — Germany's shutdown and the Diablo Canyon and Indian Point closure fights are the position in action. Every reactor produces plutonium and normalizes the enrichment and reprocessing know-how that lets states cross from civilian power to weapons — the two have never been cleanly separable, from India's 1974 test onward. High-level waste stays dangerous for hundreds of thousands of years, yet after seventy years no country operates a permanent geological repository, so "solved in principle" means our descendants inherit the practice. Piling more reactors onto a warming, geopolitically unstable world multiplies accident sites, theft targets, and proliferation pathways — and unlike a solar farm, a nuclear failure is irreversible. Cheaper, faster, catastrophically-bounded renewables let us decarbonize without betting the commons on our containment holding for millennia.
positions.proponents: M.V. Ramana, Frank von Hippel, Arjun Makhijani, Arnie Gundersen, Helen Caldicott, Kevin Kamps (Beyond Nuclear), Nuclear Information and Resource Service (NIRS), Public Citizen, Greenpeace
positions.representative_name: M.V. Ramana, "Nuclear Is Not the Solution: The Folly of Atomic Power in the Age of Climate Change" (Verso, 2024)
positions.representative_note: UBC physicist and International Panel on Fissile Materials member; argues nuclear power cannot be uncoupled from weapons proliferation, that geological waste disposal risks failure over geologic time, and that no reactor design resolves the joint problem of cost, safety, waste, and proliferation.

crux.lead: The mainstream fight is over whether the next reactor is worth building — three of the four camps would keep the running fleet; the Risk-First Skeptic would wind it down too.
crux.lead_highlight: whether the next reactor is worth building
crux.subtitle: Nuclear's clean, firm, low-death profile is broadly accepted across positions — though the Risk-First Skeptic disputes the accident death counts — and most positions would keep the plants we have, while the Risk-First Skeptic would also phase them out. The live, near-term fight is concentrated one step downstream, on new build, where it forks into two arguments usually run together: an empirical bet about cost and scale, and a values judgment about catastrophe.
crux.empirical: Whether Vogtle's ~2.6× overrun is a curable symptom of lost expertise and one-off designs, or a structural trait of the technology — and, as a separate bet, whether nuclear can add capacity fast enough to matter by 2050 against solar's ~550 GW/yr. Both are forecasts reality will grade: if standardized, repeated SMR and large-reactor builds ride costs down toward the renewables-plus-storage range, the Advocate is right and the Cost Skeptic's dollar-per-ton case weakens; if the next wave overruns like the last, or the build rate never leaves single-digit GW/yr, it holds. Both are decidable by delivered reactors — cost, schedule, and gigawatts — not by argument.
crux.values: Whether a measured death rate of ~0.03 per TWh legitimately averages away a tail — accidents, 90,000+ tonnes of stranded waste outliving any institution, proliferation — or whether some harms are categorically off-limits no matter how small their expected value. The Risk-First Skeptic and the others can agree on every number and still disagree, because this is a claim about what may be traded off, not about what is true.

actions.title: Compare energy sources on safety and carbon
actions.description: Our World in Data's evidence review: nuclear, wind and solar all cause fewer than 0.1 deaths per TWh and among the lowest lifecycle emissions, versus ~25 for coal. The shared factual floor under this whole debate.

actions.title: Back keeping the existing fleet running
actions.description: Nuclear Matters is a national coalition that lobbies policymakers to properly value existing reactors as firm, carbon-free power and to prevent premature closures. Its take-action tools contact legislators on license extensions and plant preservation.

actions.title: Join a local pro-nuclear event
actions.description: Stand Up for Nuclear is a global grassroots network that organizes rallies and community actions to protect operating plants from closure. It runs in 30-plus countries and helps supporters host or attend events in their region.

actions.title: Fund the renewables-plus-storage case
actions.description: RMI (Rocky Mountain Institute) is a nonpartisan clean-energy nonprofit that argues wind, solar and batteries deliver more decarbonization per dollar today. A 4-star Charity Navigator organization working on grid-scale clean energy portfolios.

actions.title: Read the cost-per-MWh benchmark
actions.description: Lazard's annual Levelized Cost of Energy+ is the most-cited independent estimate of what each technology costs to build. The 2025 edition finds unsubsidized renewables remain the cheapest new-build generation, the core of the cost-skeptic argument.

actions.title: Train as a nuclear advocate
actions.description: Generation Atomic's Atomic Ambassadors program equips volunteers with research and communication skills to advocate for today's reactors and the deployment of advanced ones. A grassroots 501(c)(3) that runs workshops and campaigns.

actions.title: Support advanced-nuclear policy reform
actions.description: ClearPath develops and advocates conservative-leaning federal policy to commercialize advanced reactors, including regulatory modernization and financing to drive costs down a learning curve.

actions.title: Support a nuclear-free advocacy group
actions.description: Beyond Nuclear is a 501(c)(3) campaigning for a world free of nuclear power and weapons, focused on accident risk, radioactive waste and health impacts, the strongest institutional voice for the risk-first case.

actions.title: Read the nuclear safety watchdog
actions.description: The Union of Concerned Scientists has served as an independent nuclear-safety watchdog since 1969, pressing the NRC to hold reactors to strict standards and scrutinizing waste and proliferation risks, without opposing all nuclear power.

actions.title: Add your view
actions.description: Think a position is missing, understated, or wrongly framed? Share your perspective on nuclear's role in decarbonization and help sharpen how each side is represented.

verdicts.critic: Neutrality: PASS. The draft carries asymmetry the sanctioned way — via shared Basics facts and prevalence weights — never via a house verdict. Spectrum is symmetric (+1/−1/+3/−3), Basics stats split 3 pro / 3 con / 1 neutral, and actions are exactly 2 per position with a balanced 4/4 pro-vs-skeptic split. All four steelmans are genuinely in-voice and endorsable by a real proponent (Ramana would sign the Risk-First lede as readily as the IEA would the Pragmatist), and descriptions are equal in depth and rigor. The crux is clean: it separates the empirical bet (graded symmetrically — "the Advocate is right... or it holds") from the values judgment ("can agree on every number and still disagree"), and never declares a winner. No section tilts in a way that fails the bar. The remaining items are polish, not neutrality violations.
issues: Crux lead calls new-build 'The mainstream fight' and relegates the Risk-First Skeptic's actual battleground (closing the existing fleet) to a parenthetical 'too.' This is factually defensible given prevalence, but the word 'mainstream' carries a faint normative weight that subtly marginalizes the minority position at the single highest-leverage spot in the piece for tilt.

The UCS 'learn_more' action is assigned to the Risk-First Skeptic, yet its own note admits UCS acts 'without opposing all nuclear power' — a slight mismatch, since Risk-First is the wind-it-down position. It is honest and defensible as a watchdog resource, but the representative fit is imperfect.

Aggregate prevalence leans pro-nuclear (82+64=146 vs 72+38=110). Acceptable as honest non-balance reflecting current discourse, but worth a conscious confirmation that 38 for Risk-First is a real-prevalence read and not an implicit downweighting of the anti-nuclear position.
fixes: Optional: soften the crux lead from 'The mainstream fight is over whether the next reactor is worth building' to something like 'The most active near-term fight is over whether the next reactor is worth building' — drops the 'mainstream' framing while keeping the accurate observation about where debate energy currently concentrates.

Optional: either reframe the UCS action note to present it explicitly as a safety-watchdog resource rather than the Risk-First position's voice, or swap it for a resource whose stance matches the wind-it-down position more squarely (Beyond Nuclear already fills the donate slot; a NIRS or IPFM explainer would fit learn_more better).
No change required: confirm the 38 prevalence weight for Risk-First reflects genuine current prevalence of the shut-it-all-down view; if so, leave as is — honest non-balance permits it.

verdicts.critic: Steelman review: all four positions read genuinely in-voice and each is presented as its proponents' strongest case, not a strawman or a softened placeholder. Climate Pragmatist nails the existing-fleet/cheapest-carbon argument; Cost Skeptic carries Lovins' opportunity-cost case at full strength including negative-learning; New-Nuclear Advocate makes the learning-curve/standardization bet while honestly conceding FOAK cost; Risk-First Skeptic properly refuses the death-rate-averaging frame and takes the distinctive step of opposing the existing fleet, not just new build. Asymmetry (Risk-First at 38%) is carried by prevalence weight, not by weakening the argument — which is correct. Passes the steelman bar. Two minor proponent-attribution nuances are worth tightening but do not soften any section's argument.
issues: Minor proponent/argument mismatch in Cost Skeptic: the steelman explicitly disclaims 'we're not against nuclear on principle,' but the proponent list includes Mark Z. Jacobson and Mycle Schneider, who oppose nuclear substantially on principle (risk, proliferation, weapons linkage), not on pure cost/opportunity grounds. The pure-cost version is really carried by Lovins, Lazard, and Liebreich. This is an attribution nuance, not a softened steelman.

Minor self-undercut in New-Nuclear Advocate: NuScale Power is listed as a proponent, yet why_now cites NuScale's cancelled SMR as the cautionary affordability case. Listing the flagship failed project as an exemplar proponent slightly weakens the section's own credibility to a skeptical reader, though it does not strawman the argument.
fixes: Either move Jacobson (and optionally Schneider) so their principled anti-nuclear objection isn't folded under a pure-cost banner that disclaims principled opposition, or add a half-clause acknowledging that some in this camp also object on risk grounds while Lovins/Liebreich/Lazard carry the strict dollars-per-ton version. Simplest: front the list with Lovins, Lazard, Liebreich as the representative pure-cost voices.

Drop NuScale from the New-Nuclear Advocate proponent list (or replace with the live examples already cited elsewhere: TerraPower/Natrium, X-energy, Kairos, Rolls-Royce SMR), so the section's exemplars don't include the project the draft itself uses as the cautionary tale.

verdicts.critic: Fact-source review. I web-verified all eight Basics stats plus the load-bearing figures in the questions/positions/crux. The great majority are accurate, dated, and backed by real working URLs: Vogtle ~$36.8B vs ~$14B (2.6x, Unit 4 April 2024); US capacity factor ~92% (2024); nuclear ~9% of global generation (2024, IEA); 90,000+ tonnes spent fuel growing ~2,000/yr; Lazard June 2024 nuclear $142-222, solar $29-92, wind $27-73; death rate ~0.03/TWh vs coal 24.6; solar ~550-600 GW/yr (2024); Hinkley ~£48bn; TerraPower NRC final safety eval Dec 2025 + Meta funding two units by 2032 and up to six more (~2.1 GW) by 2035. The one genuine defect is the lifecycle-carbon citation: the value 12 gCO2/kWh is the correct IPCC AR5 median, but it is sourced to the OWID safest-sources page, which now presents UNECE lifecycle data (nuclear ~5 g, below wind and solar) rather than AR5's 12 g. So the linked URL supports neither the '12 / IPCC AR5' attribution nor the note's 'on par with wind and below solar' ordering (that ranking holds only under AR5). Because a sourced stat must be backed by a URL that actually shows the value and attribution claimed, I cannot pass the carbon stat as-is.
issues: Basics stat 'Lifecycle carbon intensity' (12 gCO2/kWh): value is attributed to 'Our World in Data (IPCC AR5 lifecycle emissions)' at https://ourworldindata.org/safest-sources-of-energy, but that OWID page now presents UNECE (not IPCC AR5) lifecycle figures, under which nuclear is ~5 g and sits BELOW wind and solar. The linked URL therefore does not show the '12 g' value, does not attribute to IPCC AR5, and contradicts the note's claim that nuclear is 'on par with wind and below solar' (that ordering only holds under IPCC AR5, not under the source actually cited).

Minor: Basics 'Nuclear share of global electricity' note asserts 9% is 'its lowest share in over four decades.' The 9% (2024) is confirmed by IEA, but the 'lowest in over four decades' superlative was not directly confirmed in the IEA/Ember sources checked; plausible (peak ~17.5% in 1996) but should be explicitly sourced or softened.

Minor: Basics 'US spent fuel' 90,000+ tonnes is attributed to GAO (source_published 2024), but GAO-21-603 states ~86,000 tonnes; the current '90,000+' figure traces to DOE/2025 reporting. Attribution and date should match the source that actually states 90,000+.
fixes: Carbon stat: either (a) change the source to a page that actually shows the 12 g IPCC AR5 median (cite IPCC AR5 WG3 directly, or a source presenting the AR5 lifecycle medians), keeping value=12 and the 'on par with wind, below solar' note; or (b) keep the OWID/UNECE URL but change value to OWID's ~5 g and revise the note to 'below both wind and solar' and drop the 'IPCC AR5' label. Do not mix a UNECE-based URL with an AR5 value and an AR5-only comparison.
Nuclear-share note: add a source that states the four-decade-low claim (e.g., Ember or WNISR) or soften to 'near a multi-decade low' to match what the cited IEA URL supports.
Spent-fuel stat: set source to the DOE (or CNBC/DOE-2025) reference that states 90,000+ tonnes and date it 2025, or change the value to GAO's ~86,000 tonnes if keeping the GAO 2024 attribution.

issues: Framing tension: the subtitle says the live fight is 'concentrated one step downstream, on new build, where it forks into two arguments,' but only the empirical fork (cost curability + scale/speed) is new-build-specific. The values fork (tail risk, whether some harms are categorically off-limits) is a whole-fleet existence question — the Risk-First Skeptic contests existing reactors too, as the lead itself concedes ('would wind it down too'). Locating the values axis 'downstream, on new build' slightly mislocates it.

The lead claim 'three of the four camps would keep the running fleet' rests on the Cost Skeptic keeping existing plants. That is consistent with how the Cost Skeptic is steelmanned here (opportunity cost of new spending), but one listed proponent (Jacobson / 100% WWS) would phase out the fleet, so the claim is worth confirming for the position as a whole.
fixes: In the subtitle, distinguish the two forks by scope rather than implying both live 'on new build': e.g., keep the empirical fork as the new-build cost/scale bet, but frame the values fork as bearing on nuclear as such (existing and new), where more reactors multiply the tail — acknowledging the values disagreement is not confined downstream.

Either soften 'three of the four camps would keep the running fleet' to reflect that the Cost Skeptic's fleet stance follows from cost logic (keep cheap paid-off plants) rather than being universal among its proponents, or verify the positions section keeps the Cost Skeptic clearly pro-fleet so the crux headline stays accurate.

plan_positions.name: Climate Pragmatist
plan_positions.sketch: The existing fleet is proven, firm, low-carbon power we can't afford to lose — extend licenses, restart shuttered plants, and keep nuclear in the mix alongside renewables.

plan_positions.name: Cost Skeptic
plan_positions.sketch: Nuclear works technically but is too expensive and slow — every dollar and year buys far more decarbonization in wind, solar and storage than in new reactors.

plan_positions.name: New-Nuclear Advocate
plan_positions.sketch: Bet big on advanced reactors and SMRs — standardized, factory-built designs plus AI-driven demand and private capital will finally drive costs down a learning curve.

plan_positions.name: Risk-First Skeptic
plan_positions.sketch: Accident potential, unsolved long-lived waste and proliferation links make nuclear uniquely unacceptable — low average death rates don't capture the catastrophic tail.
